newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Netanyahu says false hopes at root of Arab anger.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu says false hopes at root of Arab anger.

text.p: Israeli leader Benjamin Netanyahu said "false dreams" were the reason for Arab anger over Israeli policies that led to an Arab League decision to suspend normal ties with the Jewish state.

He addressed parliament on Monday in a debate on a no-confidence motion over what opposition parties called Netanyahu's plunging Israel into a state of international isolation. The motion was rejected.
Netanyahu advised the Palestinians to lower their expectations.
"I want to clarify we will not retreat to the 1967 borders, we are against a Palestinian state and we actively oppose the division of Jerusalem," he said.
"I recommend abandoning false dreams. What is needed today is lowering expectations on the Palestinian side so that the gap that remains becomes bridgeable."
Arab foreign ministers, frustrated by Israeli policies on settlements and Arab territory, recommended at a meeting in Cairo ending normal relations with Israel and restoring an economic boycott.
Some ministers described the resolutions as the most decisive concerted action the Arabs had taken since Netanyahu took power last June.

Arab countries have criticised what they see as Netanyahu's brushing aside of agreements between the Palestinians and the government of his predecessor and the land-for-peace principle of peace negotiations.

The crisis in Arab-Israeli relations recently came to a head when Israeli bulldozers broke ground at a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem on March 18 and after an attack days later by a Palestinian suicide bomber in Tel Aviv which killed three Israeli women.
Palestinian protesters and Israeli troops clashed in West Bank streets for 12 days straight after the groundbreaking. One demonstrator was killed.
The United States implicitly rebuked Arab states for their decision, saying improved ties would serve the cause of peace better.
"Sustaining a regional environment supportive of peace-making is an essential part of promoting peace in the area," said State Department spokesman John Dinger.

"The United States, in fact, believes strongly that enhanced ties between Israel and her Arab neighbours contribute significantly to this goal and facilitate progress, including in the bilateral negotiations toward a comprehensive peace."
President Bill Clinton on Monday received a "sober" report on the condition of the Middle East peace process from U.S. diplomatic troubleshooter Dennis Ross, a White House spokesman said.
An official at Netanyahu's office said the prime minister was considering a visit to Washington for talks aimed at breaking the Middle East impasse.
"All possibilities are being examined," the official said without elaborating.

Israeli President Ezer Weizman was holding quiet contacts with members of the Palestinian Authority in an effort to bring Netanyahu and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat back to the negotiating table.

The director-general of Weizman's office met Palestinian Information Minister Yasser Abed Rabbo and Arafat aide Ahmed Tibi at a Jerusalem hotel on Monday to discuss arranging a meeting, one of the participants at the meeting, who declined to be identified, said.
"It was the initiative of President Weizman in order to assess the situation," he said. "He is concerned and wants to resolve the crisis."

In Dubai, Oman's Minister of State for Foreign Affairs Youssef bin Alawi bin Abdullah said his country would follow any Arab decision on relations with Israel, but did not say whether Oman would shut down Israel's trade office in Muscat.
Oman last August became the first Gulf Arab country to have any representation in Israel after opening a commercial bureau in Tel Aviv. Israel set up a similar office in Muscat.
